parts.note: points to the title of Graham Greene's 1939 thriller, whose hero is a spy on a secret mission

explanation.surface: Someone remarks that Greene kept a secret.
explanation.walkthrough: Graham Greene's novel The Confidential Agent supplies the word that 'Greene's' leaves unsaid.
explanation.definitionFit: Greene's 1939 novel is titled The Confidential Agent, so the missing noun is the spy of that title.

clue.text: She had, the guides informed him later, / Been eaten by an ——' (Ogden Nash) ()

definitions.text: She had, the guides informed him later, / Been eaten by an

parts.words: She had, the guides informed him later, / Been eaten by an
parts.note: a couplet from Ogden Nash with its last word left blank; the solver supplies the creature that rhymes with 'later'

explanation.surface: A comic verse in which a woman is swallowed by a reptile.
explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in-the-blank quotation: the missing word must complete Nash's rhyme with 'later' and begin with a vowel after 'an'.
explanation.definitionFit: Nash's rhyme for 'later' is the large swamp reptile that could swallow a person.

parts.note: The word sits just before 'Gantry' in the title

explanation.surface: Something is spotted on a crane over a Scottish island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lewis' looks like the Hebridean island and 'gantry' like a crane, but they are Sinclair Lewis and his preacher-hero's surname.
explanation.definitionFit: In Sinclair Lewis's 1927 novel the title preacher's first name comes before his surname Gantry.

definitions.meaning: in the song 'Rule, Britannia!' Britannia rules the sea's rollers

explanation.surface: A Woolf novel is published under British rule.
explanation.definitionFit: Woolf wrote The Waves, and the patriotic song says Britannia rules the waves, the ocean she governs.

indicators.note: something unusual is out of its normal order, so the letters of these two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: An offprint of an odd poetic muse stands on its own.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unusual' rearranges the letters of MUSE and APART together.
explanation.definitionFit: An offprint is a separately printed copy of an article, which bibliographers call by the Latin term for 'something separated'.

clue.text: Dream sequence joiner suggests tight fit

definitions.meaning: in A Midsummer Night's Dream the joiner (carpenter) among the mechanicals plays the Lion

explanation.surface: A carpenter in a dream sequence finds things fit closely.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's joiner in the Dream is named Snug, and a garment that is close-fitting is said to be snug.

clue.text: Possibly help a vegetable definition of Eastern chasuble

indicators.note: possibly suggests the letters might be arranged in another way, signalling an anagram

parts.note: an onion is a common vegetable

explanation.surface: Someone offers vegetable help with defining an Easter vestment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Possibly' marks the anagram; 'vegetable' looks like part of the surface's odd phrase but supplies the second piece. The vestment is also spelt phelonion.
explanation.definitionFit: The phaelonion is the sleeveless outer vestment worn by priests in the Orthodox church, its equivalent of the Western chasuble.

parts.note: read as Engineers', i.e. RE's: RE is the Royal Engineers plus the possessive S
a cue is a prompt to an actor

explanation.surface: Engineers give a signal for Conrad to be saved.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'Engineers' as a possessive (the Royal Engineers'), so the S is a letter, not a plural; Conrad's novel The Rescue makes the definition literary.
explanation.definitionFit: Saving from danger is deliverance, and Joseph Conrad wrote a novel titled The Rescue.

parts.note: the first names of the English historian G. M. ..., great-nephew of Lord Macaulay

explanation.surface: A historian is named by his first names.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Macaulay' looks like the historian Thomas Babington Macaulay, but here it is a middle name of his great-nephew.
explanation.definitionFit: George Macaulay is the forename pair of the twentieth-century English historian surnamed Trevelyan.

clue.text: American dramatist presents adaptation of Emma on time

indicators.note: in a down entry one piece sitting on another comes before it
an adaptation reshapes the original, so the letters of the novel's title are rearranged

explanation.surface: A US playwright puts on a stage version of Jane Austen's Emma.
explanation.walkthrough: 'adaptation of' rearranges EMMA into MAME, and 'on' puts that above T in the down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: David Mamet is the US playwright of Glengarry Glen Ross.

clue.text: His work is not expected to change its spots

definitions.text: His work is not expected to change its spots

parts.words: His work is not expected to change its spots
parts.note: the proverb says a leopard cannot change its spots; this author wrote The Leopard

explanation.surface: Someone whose output never alters its markings.
explanation.walkthrough: Giuseppe Tomasi di Lampedusa wrote Il Gattopardo (The Leopard), and the proverb says a leopard cannot change its spots.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sicilian novelist wrote The Leopard, and a leopard proverbially keeps its spotted coat.

indicators.note: changed means the letters are put into a different order

explanation.surface: Shipmates are swapped aboard a boat in a John Galt story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'changed' rearranges MATES. John Galt, the Scottish novelist, wrote The Steam-Boat, so the answer sits in the name of Galt's vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: Galt's novel The Steam-Boat names a vessel powered by water vapour, the first part of that title.

indicators.note: in signals that the letters lie inside the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: A musician in peril manages to get away.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters sit inside 'danGER MANages'; 'escape' completes the picture of slipping out from those words.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Edward German was an English composer of light opera such as Merrie England.

parts.note: Sartre's long study L'Idiot de la famille is about a nineteenth-century French novelist

explanation.surface: Sartre calls one of his relatives a fool.
explanation.walkthrough: Sartre's L'Idiot de la famille (The Family Idiot) is a vast biography of the author of Madame Bovary.
explanation.definitionFit: Sartre's multi-volume study titled The Family Idiot takes the author of Madame Bovary as its subject.

clue.text: His work not expected to endure?

definitions.text: His work not expected to endure?

parts.words: His work not expected to endure?
parts.note: a writer of short-lived things, such as journals or works on what lasts a day

explanation.surface: A writer whose output will not last.
explanation.definitionFit: Something ephemeral lasts only a day, so a writer of transient material is named from that Greek root.

clue.text: £25 on the socialist work of Steinbeck

indicators.note: in an across entry, A on B puts A after B

parts.note: red is the colour and nickname of a socialist
pony is British slang for twenty-five pounds

explanation.surface: Someone bets £25 on the left-wing candidate in a Steinbeck story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' is a betting word in the surface but signals order here; a pony is British slang for twenty-five pounds.
explanation.definitionFit: Steinbeck's 1937 novella about a boy and his horse is titled with a colour and a small horse.

definitions.meaning: Longfellow, whose surname suggests a tall man, wrote a poem with this title

explanation.surface: A tall poet climbs higher.
explanation.walkthrough: Longfellow is 'apparently tall' because his name reads as 'long fellow'; his poem has the Latin title meaning 'higher'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin word means 'higher still', and it is the title of a well-known Longfellow poem.

indicators.note: in shows the letters sit within the phrase fancy masonry

explanation.surface: A cornice moulding set in decorative stonework.
explanation.definitionFit: An S-shaped moulding of a cornice, with ogee profile, is the architects' cyma.

parts.note: Byron's line 'The Assyrian came down like the wolf on the fold'

explanation.surface: A group that swooped down like wolves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lupine' means wolf-like: Byron's The Destruction of Sennacherib opens with the ancient army coming down like a wolf on the fold.
explanation.definitionFit: In Byron's poem the ancient Mesopotamian army descends like a wolf upon sheep.

clue.text: Stage hum surprisingly produced by Fowles sorcerer

indicators.note: surprisingly hints that the letters turn up in an unexpected order

explanation.surface: A stage hum is unexpectedly produced by a magician from a Fowles novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'surprisingly' rearranges STAGE HUM.
explanation.definitionFit: John Fowles's novel The Magus centres on a manipulative magician figure on a Greek island.

clue.text: The sort of music for Eliot piece

definitions.meaning: T. S. Eliot's 1934 pageant play The ...

explanation.surface: A type of music is chosen for an Eliot work.
explanation.definitionFit: Rock is a genre of popular music, and Eliot wrote the pageant play The Rock.

indicators.note: wrecked means broken up, so the letters of the phrase are rearranged

explanation.surface: A wrecked shop annexe exposes a thinker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wrecked' rearranges SHOP ANNEXE.
explanation.definitionFit: Xenophanes of Colophon was a pre-Socratic Greek thinker and poet.

definitions.meaning: In French the word means the second crop of hay, an aftermath

explanation.surface: Recovering what follows a Giono novel.
explanation.definitionFit: To recover something is to win it again, and Giono's novel Regain takes its title from the French term for the second mowing of hay.

clue.text: "What man can pretend to be a in love, who is an abjurer of wine?" (R. B. Sheridan)

definitions.text: What man can pretend to be a in love, who is an abjurer of wine?

parts.words: What man can pretend to be a in love, who is an abjurer of wine?
parts.note: a line from Sheridan's The School for Scandal with a word missing after 'a': someone who has faith

explanation.surface: Sheridan asks how a teetotaller can claim to be in love.
explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in-the-blank quotation from Sheridan; the blank follows 'a' and fits 'in love'.
explanation.definitionFit: Sheridan's line asks who can claim to have faith in love while forswearing wine.

parts.note: iris and daisy are flowers, while Molly and Leopold are the married couple in Joyce's Ulysses

explanation.surface: A list of four first names.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Iris' and 'Daisy' look like women's names but are flowers; Molly and Leopold are the couple at the heart of Joyce's Ulysses.
explanation.definitionFit: A flower is a blossom, which covers iris and daisy, and Joyce's Molly and Leopold share that surname.

clue.text: Slow-moving novelist rose without a start

indicators.note: without a start says the first letter of the rose name is removed

parts.note: a rambler is a climbing rose

explanation.surface: A sluggish novelist's rose loses its opening bud.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without a start' takes R off RAMBLER. Eric Ambler wrote spy thrillers, and one who strolls slowly is also an ambler.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who walks at a leisurely pace strolls, and Eric Ambler was a British thriller writer.

clue.text: Colin Davis includes Trollope's eponymous heroine

indicators.note: includes shows the name Colin Davis holds the letters within it

explanation.surface: The conductor Colin Davis includes a Trollope heroine in a programme.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters sit inside 'coLIN DAvis'. Trollope's novel Linda Tressel is named after its heroine.
explanation.definitionFit: Trollope's 1868 novel Linda Tressel takes its title from its heroine's name.

parts.note: Bulwer-Lytton wrote a poem called The Siamese Twins; bring 'Siamese' up to date and it becomes the modern name for the people of that land

explanation.surface: A modern portrait of the novelist Bulwer.
explanation.walkthrough: Bulwer-Lytton's satire The Siamese Twins is the link: Siam is now Thailand, so 'Siamese' updated gives the modern adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Siam was renamed Thailand in 1939, so the modern word for Siamese describes Bulwer's poem title.

clue.text: Franco-Russian agreement suggested by Louise Ramé

parts.note: oui is French for yes
da is Russian for yes

explanation.surface: A Franco-Russian treaty is hinted at by a Victorian lady novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'agreement' is saying yes: OUI in French, DA in Russian.
explanation.definitionFit: Maria Louise Ramé wrote under the pen name Ouida, her childish way of saying Louisa.

parts.note: O'Neill's play Mourning Becomes Electra; Electra's sister was sacrificed by Agamemnon

explanation.surface: A woman whose sister grieves gracefully.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mourned becomingly' points to O'Neill's Mourning Becomes Electra, so the sister is Electra; her sister was sacrificed at Aulis by their father Agamemnon.
explanation.definitionFit: Electra, of O'Neill's title, was the sister of Agamemnon's sacrificed daughter in Greek myth.

clue.text: Italian futurist creates jolly dancing bird

parts.note: jolly is old naval slang for a Royal Marine

indicators.note: dancing jumbles the letters of the bird's name

parts.note: a tit is a small bird

explanation.surface: An Italian futurist makes a cheerful bird dance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'jolly' is not cheerful but Royal Navy slang for a Marine; 'dancing' rearranges TIT into TTI.
explanation.definitionFit: Filippo Tommaso Marinetti wrote the 1909 Futurist Manifesto.

clue.text: Yeats's wild ones looking pale, taken in ——'

definitions.text: Yeats's wild ones looking pale, taken in

parts.words: Yeats's wild ones looking pale, taken in
parts.note: Yeats's poem The Wild ... at Coole names the wild birds

explanation.surface: Yeats's wild creatures look pale and are deceived.
explanation.walkthrough: Yeats wrote The Wild Swans at Coole; the clue's remaining words are a quotation with its last word missing.
explanation.definitionFit: Yeats's poem names the wild white birds on the lake at Coole.
